title: New US Bill Would End OPT, Kill H-1B Green Card Pathway in Sweeping Overhaul
excerpt: Rep. Chip Roy’s American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act targets every stage of the Indian professional immigration pipeline, from student work permits to permanent residency
body:
A new bill introduced by Republican Congressman Chip Roy of Texas aims to fundamentally reshape the H-1B visa program — and if passed, it would dismantle several pathways that hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals have relied on for decades to build careers and lives in the United States.

The American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act of 2026 would replace the current H-1B lottery with a wage-based selection system, eliminate the Optional Practical Training program used by international students after graduation, end the use of H-1B visas as a pathway to permanent residency, and bar companies that have recently conducted layoffs from hiring H-1B workers.

## What the Bill Would Change

The legislation targets four pillars of the current immigration system that Indian professionals and students have depended upon.

**Lottery replaced by wages.** The bill would scrap the existing H-1B lottery — under which roughly 780,000 applications competed for 85,000 slots in 2025 — and replace it with a system that awards visas to candidates commanding the highest salaries. The stated goal is to ensure H-1B slots go to genuinely specialized roles rather than entry-level positions.

**OPT eliminated.** The Optional Practical Training program, which allows F-1 student visa holders to work in the US for up to three years after graduation (12 months standard plus a 24-month STEM extension), would be abolished entirely. OPT has served as the primary bridge between American universities and the US job market for international students — a pipeline through which tens of thousands of Indians transition each year.

**Green card pathway severed.** Currently, employers can sponsor H-1B holders for permanent residency (a green card) while they continue working. The bill would end this practice, effectively making the H-1B a strictly temporary work visa with no avenue to settle permanently.

**Layoff-hire ban.** Companies that have conducted layoffs would be prohibited from filing H-1B petitions — a direct response to the widespread criticism that major tech firms have laid off American workers while simultaneously expanding their H-1B workforce.

## The Political Context

Roy framed the legislation as a defence of American STEM workers. “For its nearly forty-year history, the H-1B visa has been abused, allowing employers to routinely sideline American STEM workers in favour of cheap foreign labour, while masking layoffs and wage suppression as ‘shortages,’” he said.

The bill builds on companion legislation from Rep. Eli Crane of Arizona, whose End H-1B Visa Abuse Act of 2026 proposes a three-year pause on H-1B visa issuances followed by broader reforms. Together, the two bills represent the most aggressive Congressional push to restructure the H-1B program in years.

Meanwhile, Senator Jim Banks of Indiana has introduced the American Tech Workforce Act in the Senate, which would raise the H-1B wage floor from $60,000 to $150,000, eliminate OPT, and replace the lottery with an auction system. The convergence of multiple bills from different lawmakers signals growing momentum in Congress for H-1B restrictions, even as the courts separately battle the Trump administration’s $100,000 H-1B fee.

## Prospects and Industry Reaction

Despite the aggressive rhetoric, immigration policy experts note that comprehensive H-1B reform bills have historically struggled to advance beyond committee stage. The tech industry — which employs the vast majority of H-1B holders — has consistently lobbied against restrictions, arguing that visa holders fill genuine skill gaps.

The US Chamber of Commerce and major tech employers are expected to oppose the bill, as they have done with similar proposals. But the political headwinds facing H-1B workers have intensified: the Trump administration’s $100,000 fee (currently blocked by a federal judge in Boston), investigations into OPT-related fraud involving more than 10,000 students, and a steady drumbeat of layoff-and-replace stories in the tech sector have shifted public opinion.

## The Diaspora Impact

For Indian professionals, the bill represents a worst-case convergence: losing the lottery system many have navigated for years, losing OPT as a post-graduation safety net, and losing the H-1B-to-green-card pipeline that has defined the Indian immigration pathway since the 1990s.

Indians account for roughly 72 percent of all H-1B visas issued annually, and the green card backlog for Indian applicants already stretches beyond 100 years in some employment categories. Severing the H-1B-to-green-card link would leave tens of thousands of Indian workers in permanent limbo — legally employed but with no route to permanent settlement.

Advocacy groups are already mobilising. Immigration attorney and community leader Ajay Bhutoria has said organisations are preparing potential legal challenges should any version of these proposals advance.

The bill has been referred to the House Judiciary Committee. Whether it gains traction will depend on broader immigration negotiations and the Republican caucus’s willingness to pursue restrictions that could face strong opposition from the business wing of the party.

*Sources: Roy.house.gov, Daily Caller, Times of India, Texas Politics*
